content.overview: Crop steering uses intentional changes in irrigation and environmental strategy to influence root-zone conditions and plant response. Advanced steering should be treated as an evidence-controlled feedback process, not as a fixed recipe copied across facilities.

vocabulary.definition: Intentional management of irrigation and environmental inputs to influence root-zone trajectories and plant response.
Adjustment based on measured response rather than only predetermined schedule.
A predefined measurement used to judge whether a steering change had the intended effect.

sections.title: Start from a measured baseline
sections.body: Before changing strategy, establish root-zone water content, dryback, input/return chemistry, delivery uniformity and environmental context so the effect of the change can be interpreted.

sections.title: Change one interpretable variable when possible
sections.body: Simultaneous changes to volume, frequency, feed concentration and environment make it difficult to identify which change produced the observed response.

sections.title: Use response, not folklore, to validate steering
sections.body: Substrate and crop response differ by system. A published or vendor steering schedule is a hypothesis until validated under the facility's cultivar, media, climate and irrigation hardware.

workedExamples: A facility increases event frequency while holding event volume constant and then compares dryback, return EC and crop response before making a second change.
commonMistakes: Changing volume, frequency and feed EC together.
Treating a vendor chart as universal.
Calling a steering change successful because the intended schedule ran.
content.practicalApplication: Design a controlled steering trial with baseline, single planned change, expected response, monitoring interval and stop/escalation criteria.
content.summary: Crop steering is strongest when it behaves like a controlled experiment with measurable response and explicit limits.
